Three-point estimating addresses uncertainty: triangular E = (O + M + P) / 3; beta (PERT) E = (O + 4M + P) / 6, which weights the most likely estimate more. The county, the portal, the fee law, the estimates, the budget, the weekly planned value, the progress each event moves and the trust gauges are teaching figures for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the project manager for Riverbend County, a fictional county, building an online building-permit portal. A new state fee law starts on Monday 3 April 2028 and the portal must calculate and collect its fees from that day. The budget is 360 thousand dollars over 12 weeks from Monday 10 January 2028.
handover: Sponsor: Helen Ortiz, county administrator. Product owner for the residents' application wizard: Raj Patel, permits manager. A team of six developers and two testers.
Planned value is 30 thousand dollars a week; the dashboard shows PV, EV, AC, SPI and CPI at each Friday status meeting.
howItWorks: The dashboard shows the objective, the approach and the budget, the work, earned value against plan, the open issues, the people and the milestones.
Move the project on a week at a time. Decisions come to you as they arise; before them you can read the law or talk to the people who apply for permits.
At go-live you close the project and write a short note.

approachPrompt.title: End of week 1: which delivery approach?
approachPrompt.context: The fee module must match a schedule fixed in law by a fixed date. The application wizard's needs are unclear: counter staff and contractors disagree on what residents need first. The parcel lookup depends on an old county GIS service.

choices.label: Recommend a hybrid approach: plan and baseline the fee module and the GIS work predictively; build the wizard in two-week iterations with the permits manager as product owner, to the fixed release date; tie both into one integrated plan

effects.log: Approved: a hybrid plan, with one schedule and one budget across both parts.

choices.feedback: The approach follows each part's complexity and certainty: fixed, well-understood requirements suit a predictive plan; uncertain ones suit iterations; a hybrid ties them into one plan.

choices.label: Specify and baseline everything up front, the wizard included

effects.log: The wizard is specified in full before anyone has tried it.

choices.feedback: Specifying uncertain needs up front plans rework in.

choices.label: Run everything in iterations with no baseline, the fee module included

effects.log: No baseline for the fee module.

choices.feedback: A part fixed in law, with a fixed date, needs a plan and a baseline it can be accepted against.

estimatePrompt.title: End of week 2: estimating the work
estimatePrompt.context: The GIS integration is the uncertain piece: the team's optimistic, most likely and pessimistic figures are 8, 12 and 22 days. The 40 permit forms take about 2 days each. Last year's portal in another county took 10 days for its GIS work. The GIS vendor says 8.

choices.label: Use a three-point (PERT) estimate for the GIS work, (8 + 4 x 12 + 22) / 6 = 13 days, and a parametric estimate for the forms, 40 x 2 = 80 days of effort

effects.log: The plan carries 13 days for the GIS work and 80 days of effort for the forms.

choices.feedback: Uncertain work gets a three-point estimate; repeatable units get a parametric one.

choices.label: Use last year's portal: 10 days for the GIS work
choices.feedback: Analogous estimating is quick but only as good as the likeness; this county's GIS is older.

choices.label: Take the vendor's 8 days
choices.feedback: The optimistic figure alone is not an estimate of uncertain work.

changePrompt.title: End of week 5: the state amends the law
changePrompt.context: The legislature adds a requirement: permit applicants must be offered inspection scheduling from the start date. It touches the wizard, the GIS lookup and the fee module, and needs about 20 thousand dollars of work.

choices.label: Assess the impact across scope, schedule, cost, risk and communications, take it to change control, and update the integrated plan, the fee module's baseline and the wizard's backlog together

effects.log: Approved with its impact: the plan, the baseline and the backlog all updated, funded from the schedule and budget reserves.

choices.feedback: An integrated plan is maintained as a whole: a change's impact is assessed across every subsidiary plan, decided through change control, and the documents updated together.

choices.label: Add it to the wizard backlog; the team will fit it in
choices.feedback: A change that touches three parts changed in one plan leaves the others wrong.

choices.label: Leave it until after launch; the scope is baselined
choices.feedback: A legal requirement with a start date is not optional scope; the baseline is changed through control.

velocityPrompt.title: End of week 8: the wizard will not finish everything
velocityPrompt.context: Four iterations in, the wizard's velocity forecasts about 70% of the backlog by the release date. The fee module is in testing and on its baseline.

choices.label: Reprioritize with the permits manager: agree the must-haves for launch (apply, upload, pay, schedule an inspection), move the rest after launch, and update the integrated plan and the stakeholders

effects.log: Launch scope agreed; the remainder planned for May.

choices.feedback: In the adaptive part, scope flexes to the fixed date by value, with the product owner; the integrated plan reflects it.

choices.label: Add two developers for the last four weeks
choices.feedback: Adding people late adds onboarding and coordination before it adds output.

choices.label: Move the fee module's testers onto the wizard

effects.log: Fee module testing is cut short.

choices.feedback: The legally fixed part is the one that must be accepted against the law.

reflection.question: Write the close-out note for the sponsor: the approach you recommended and why, how the work was estimated, and how the plan was kept integrated through the amendment and the wizard's forecast.

parts.label: Approach and estimates
parts.criteria: Recommends a hybrid from the parts' differing certainty; uses three-point estimating for the uncertain GIS work (13 days) and parametric for the forms.
parts.modelAnswer: The fee module was fixed in law with a fixed date, so it was planned and baselined; the wizard's needs were unknown, so it ran in iterations to the release date, all in one plan. The GIS work was estimated at (8 + 48 + 22) / 6 = 13 days; the forms at 40 x 2 days.

parts.label: Keeping the plan integrated
parts.criteria: Takes the amendment through change control with its impact on every subsidiary plan; flexes the wizard's scope to the date with the product owner; keeps the fee module's testing.
parts.modelAnswer: The amendment touched three parts: we assessed it across the plans, it was approved, and the baseline and backlog were updated together. At 70% forecast we agreed the launch must-haves with the permits manager and planned the rest for May.

scoring.modelReasoning: Assess complexity part by part: a fee module fixed in law with a fixed date suits a predictive, baselined plan; a wizard whose needs are unknown suits iterations to a fixed release date; a hybrid integrates them in one schedule and budget. Estimate uncertain work with three points, (O + 4M + P) / 6 = 13 days here, and repeatable work parametrically, 40 forms x 2 days. Maintain the integrated plan as a whole: a legal amendment touching three parts is assessed across scope, schedule, cost, risk and communications, decided through change control, and the baseline and backlog updated together. In the adaptive part, scope flexes to the date by value with the product owner; the legally fixed part keeps its testing.
